newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court rules against Perot on debate exclusion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court rules against Perot on debate exclusion.

text.p: A federal appeals court Friday rejected a last-ditch emergency appeal by Texas billionaire Ross Perot and another third-party presidential candidate over their exclusion from the presidential debates.

Just two days before President Bill Clinton and Republican rival Bob Dole hold their first debate in Hartford, Connecticut, the three appellate judges upheld a lower court ruling that rejected Perot's arguments.

Reform Party candidate Perot and John Hagelin of the Natural Law Party had sued the Federal Election Commission, a government agency, and a bipartisan commission in an attempt to force their way into the nationally televised debates.

They charged that the Commission on Presidential Debates violated Federal Election Commission rules that require "objective" criteria in selecting the debaters and claimed their candidates qualified under rules used since 1988.

The unanimous appeals court ruling affirmed all but one minor part of a ruling Tuesday by U.S. District Judge Thomas Hogan, who held that Perot and Hagelin had failed to prove that their exclusion violated the law.

"In sum, we are unpersuaded that the (Federal Election Commission) has unconstitutionally delegated legislative authority to the (debates commission)," the appeals court concluded in a 16-page ruling rejecting Perot's arguments.
